story.title: US Boycotts UN Human Rights Review, Meeting Postponed
story.summary: The United States has opted out of a key UN human rights review for the second consecutive year, leading to the postponement of the meeting until January. The US government stated that participation would imply support for the UN Human Rights Council, which it has criticized as ineffective. Rights organizations have expressed concern that this absence could weaken global accountability for human rights issues.

explore_lenses.label: Why does the U.S. absence matter?
explore_lenses.title: A universal review loses the country’s direct response
explore_lenses.summary: The Universal Periodic Review (UPR) is designed to subject every UN member state to peer scrutiny, using government, UN, and civil-society material. The U.S. absence does not erase the evidence submitted about its record, but it prevents U.S. officials from answering questions and responding to recommendations in the normal forum.

claims.text: The UPR reviews each UN member state’s human-rights record roughly every 4.5 years; the process draws on a national report, an OHCHR compilation of UN information, and an OHCHR summary of credible stakeholder submissions.

The U.S. had completed three prior UPR reviews, including its third review in 2020; the State Department previously described the process as distinct from membership in the 47-state Human Rights Council because non-members also participate in reviews.

Human Rights Watch argues that a second U.S. failure to appear is unprecedented in the UPR’s nearly 20-year history and says the Council should not allow the U.S. to be exempted from a process intended to apply to all UN members.

points: The UPR reviews each UN member state’s human-rights record roughly every 4.5 years; the process draws on a national report, an OHCHR compilation of UN information, and an OHCHR summary of credible stakeholder submissions.

The U.S. had completed three prior UPR reviews, including its third review in 2020; the State Department previously described the process as distinct from membership in the 47-state Human Rights Council because non-members also participate in reviews.

Human Rights Watch argues that a second U.S. failure to appear is unprecedented in the UPR’s nearly 20-year history and says the Council should not allow the U.S. to be exempted from a process intended to apply to all UN members.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The UPR is a peer-review mechanism rather than a court, and it is unclear what practical leverage the Council will use if the United States again declines to participate.

explore_lenses.label: How did this reach a second boycott?
explore_lenses.title: Withdrawal policy was extended to the review process
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate backdrop is the Trump administration’s 2025 decision to withdraw from and stop funding the Human Rights Council. Although the UPR can formally involve non-Council members, the administration has treated participation in the review as inconsistent with its broader policy toward the Council.

claims.text: Executive Order 14199, issued February 4, 2025, directed U.S. withdrawal from the Human Rights Council and stated that the Council had allowed human-rights abusers to shield themselves from scrutiny while acting against U.S. interests and allies.
The U.S. fourth-cycle review was initially scheduled for November 7, 2025 and was postponed to November 10, 2026 after the first no-show.

In its November 2026 coverage, NPR reported that the State Department described the Council as pushing anti-American rhetoric, while rights advocates argued that the refusal reflects a broader retreat from multilateral accountability mechanisms.

The U.S. fourth-cycle review was initially scheduled for November 7, 2025 and was postponed to November 10, 2026 after the first no-show.

In its November 2026 coverage, NPR reported that the State Department described the Council as pushing anti-American rhetoric, while rights advocates argued that the refusal reflects a broader retreat from multilateral accountability mechanisms.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The administration has not indicated that it will revoke its policy before the rescheduled review.

explore_lenses.label: What happens before the January deadline?
explore_lenses.title: The Council has rescheduled the case, not closed it
explore_lenses.summary: The Human Rights Council has postponed rather than cancelled the U.S. review and asked its president to continue efforts to obtain U.S. cooperation. That keeps open a route for U.S. participation, but also leaves the Council facing a decision about how to handle continuing non-cooperation.

claims.text: The Council expressed regret over continued U.S. non-cooperation, urged the United States to resume participation, and asked its president to take appropriate steps to encourage cooperation.
The Council rescheduled the U.S. UPR for the Working Group’s January 18-29, 2027 session and said it would consider additional appropriate steps before that session ends.

Human Rights Watch had urged the Council to proceed with scrutiny without granting another extension, whereas UN participants cited by NPR worried that holding a review without the country under review could create a precedent other governments might follow.

Human Rights Watch had urged the Council to proceed with scrutiny without granting another extension, whereas UN participants cited by NPR worried that holding a review without the country under review could create a precedent other governments might follow.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: It remains unresolved whether Washington will attend in January 2027 and what “additional appropriate steps” the Council will adopt if it does not.

story_report.summary: The United States has skipped its UN human-rights review for a second consecutive year, prompting the Human Rights Council to postpone the session to its Jan. 18-29, 2027 working-group meeting. U.S. officials have said taking part would imply support for the Council, which the administration has criticized. The Council expressed regret over Washington’s continued non-cooperation and urged it to return to the review process.

sections.heading: Universal Periodic Review Process
sections.body: The Universal Periodic Review examines every UN member state’s human-rights record about once every 4.5 years. It draws on a national report, an Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights compilation of UN material, and a summary of credible stakeholder submissions. The United States had completed three prior reviews, most recently in 2020, and the State Department had previously described the process as separate from membership in the 47-member Human Rights Council.

sections.heading: Washington’s Council Objections
sections.body: The administration’s position follows Executive Order 14199, issued in February 2025, directing U.S. withdrawal from the Human Rights Council. The order said the Council had enabled human-rights abusers to avoid scrutiny while acting against U.S. interests and allies. NPR reported that the State Department characterized the Council as advancing anti-American rhetoric, while rights advocates said the refusal represented a broader retreat from multilateral accountability mechanisms.

sections.heading: Council Response and Criticism
sections.body: The fourth-cycle U.S. review was originally scheduled for Nov. 7, 2025 and moved to Nov. 10, 2026 after the first U.S. absence. Human Rights Watch called a second failure to appear unprecedented in the review’s nearly 20-year history and argued that the United States should not be exempted from a process intended for all UN members. The group urged continued scrutiny without another extension, while UN participants cited by NPR warned that reviewing a country in its absence could set a precedent for other governments.

unresolved.text: It remains unclear whether Washington will participate in January 2027 or what additional steps the Council will take if it again declines; the review is a peer-review mechanism rather than a court.

related_stories.title: Pope Leo XIV Continues Latin American Tour with Visit to Argentina
related_stories.summary: Pope Leo XIV is currently visiting Argentina as part of his 12-day South American tour, following a stop in Uruguay. During his visit, he celebrated public Masses, met with the faithful, and engaged in discussions with religious and government leaders. The pontiff received a warm welcome from crowds in Claypole, near Buenos Aires, where he visited the Don Orione care home and unveiled a plaque.

related_stories.title: Teddy Riner Announces Presidential Bid in France
related_stories.summary: Teddy Riner, the 37-year-old Olympic judo champion, has declared his candidacy for the French presidency in the 2027 election. He made the announcement via social media, amid a political landscape where public opinion is divided between far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and far-right candidate Marine Le Pen.

related_stories.title: Explosion at Turkey Steel Factory Claims 17 Lives
related_stories.summary: A powerful explosion at the Habaş iron and steelworks in Aliağa, Izmir province, Turkey, has resulted in the deaths of at least 17 people. Eyewitnesses reported that the blast felt like an earthquake, with flames and thick smoke visible from the site. Distressed relatives gathered outside the factory following the incident.
